## Setup

`pdftools` uses the Poppler C++ library, so unlike `tabulapdf` it doesn't need
Java. The CRAN binaries for macOS and Windows include Poppler. On Linux,
install `libpoppler-cpp-dev` first.

`pdftools` has no table detector. It gives you two things to work with:

- `pdf_text()`: one string per page, laid out with spaces to roughly match
  the printed page.
- `pdf_data()`: every word on a page with its x/y position.

The sections below build tables from each of these.

```{r}
#| label: setup
# install.packages(c("pdftools", "tidyverse", "janitor"))
library(pdftools)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

# This .qmd lives in data/, alongside the PDF
pdf_path <- "fy2027greenbooknps_0.pdf"
file.exists(pdf_path)
```

## Get to know the document

The Greenbook is long, so first figure out which pages hold the tables you want.

```{r}
#| label: metadata
pdf_length(pdf_path)
pdf_info(pdf_path)[c("pages", "created", "producer")]
pdf_pagesize(pdf_path)[1, ]     # width/height in PDF points
```

Pull out the raw text of every page and search it for keywords to find
the pages you want.

```{r}
#| label: find-pages
page_text <- pdf_text(pdf_path)              # one string per page

pages_tbl <- tibble(
  page = seq_along(page_text),
  text = page_text
)

# Change the pattern to whatever table you're after
find_pages <- function(pattern) {
  pages_tbl |>
    filter(str_detect(text, regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
    pull(page)
}

find_pages("Summary of Requirements")
find_pages("Park Base Funding|Park Management")
```

## Approach 1: split the page text on whitespace

`pdf_text()` keeps the page layout, so columns are usually separated by
runs of two or more spaces. Splitting on those runs works for most
whitespace-only budget tables, like Tabula's `"stream"` mode does.

```{r}
#| label: single-page-text
test_page <- find_pages("Summary of Requirements")[1]   # or set a number

cat(page_text[[test_page]])    # look at the raw layout first

text_table <- function(p, min_gap = 2) {
  lines <- str_split_1(page_text[[p]], "\n") |> str_trim()
  lines <- lines[lines != ""]

  cells <- str_split(lines, sprintf("\\s{%d,}", min_gap))
  n_col <- max(lengths(cells))

  cells |>
    map(\(x) c(x, rep(NA_character_, n_col - length(x)))) |>
    do.call(what = rbind) |>
    as_tibble(.name_repair = \(nm) paste0("x", seq_along(nm))) |>
    mutate(.page = p, .before = 1)
}

tbl_text <- text_table(test_page)
tbl_text
```

This approach has one weakness. When a row has an empty cell, the values
after it shift left into the wrong column. If that happens, use the
coordinate approach below.

## Approach 2: use word coordinates

`pdf_data()` returns one row per word with `x`, `y`, `width`, and `height`
in PDF points, measured from the top-left corner. Plot the words to see
where the table sits and where the column boundaries fall.

```{r}
#| label: word-positions
words <- pdf_data(pdf_path)[[test_page]]
words

ggplot(words, aes(x, y, label = text)) +
  geom_text(size = 2, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = seq(0, 800, 50)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 650, 50)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Read off from the plot:

- `area` is `c(top, left, bottom, right)`, the box around the table, so
  page headers and footers are left out.
- `col_breaks` are the x positions where each new column starts. Put them
  in the gaps between columns.

```{r}
#| label: coord-table
words_to_table <- function(words, col_breaks, area = NULL, y_tol = 3) {
  if (!is.null(area)) {
    words <- words |>
      filter(y >= area[1], x >= area[2],
             y + height <= area[3], x + width <= area[4])
  }

  words |>
    arrange(y, x) |>
    mutate(
      row = cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(y) > y_tol)),   # same line if y within y_tol
      col = findInterval(x, col_breaks) + 1
    ) |>
    arrange(row, col, x) |>
    summarise(text = str_c(text, collapse = " "), .by = c(row, col)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = text,
                names_prefix = "x", names_sort = TRUE) |>
    select(-row)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: coord-example
#| eval: false
words_to_table(
  words,
  col_breaks = c(250, 330, 410, 490),     # adjust to your table
  area       = c(100, 30, 720, 590)       # adjust to your table
)
```

## Extract from many pages

Once one page looks right, loop over a range of pages. The `.page` column
records where each table came from.

```{r}
#| label: many-pages
target_pages <- find_pages("Summary of Requirements")

raw_tables <- map(target_pages, text_table)

# If the pages share a layout, the coordinate approach also works in a loop:
# all_words  <- pdf_data(pdf_path)
# raw_tables <- map(target_pages, \(p) {
#   words_to_table(all_words[[p]], col_breaks = c(250, 330, 410, 490)) |>
#     mutate(.page = p, .before = 1)
# })

length(raw_tables)
```

## Clean up

Budget tables usually need a few standard fixes: clean the column names,
strip `$` and `,` from numbers, and treat dashes as zero or NA.

```{r}
#| label: clean
clean_budget_table <- function(df) {
  df |>
    clean_names() |>
    mutate(across(
      -c(1:2),   # keep .page and the label column as text
      \(x) x |>
        str_replace_all("[$,]", "") |>
        str_replace("^[-–—]+$", NA_character_) |>
        str_replace("^\\((.*)\\)$", "-\\1") |>      # (123) -> -123
        parse_number()
    ))
}

cleaned <- map(raw_tables, possibly(clean_budget_table, otherwise = NULL)) |>
  compact()

cleaned[[1]]
```

## Save

```{r}
#| label: save
#| eval: false
iwalk(cleaned, \(df, i) write_csv(df, sprintf("greenbook_table_%03d.csv", i)))
```
